To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
retrogressive deformation and metamorphic overprinting in the footwall of the metamorphic complex are common, but their importance for exhumation is still insufficiently emphasized.

retrogressive deformation within a metamorphic core complex may pervade the entire core complex, and that the temporal range of retrogressive deformation may span the entire duration of core complex exhumation.

retrogressive deformation in the footwall of metamorphic core complex is not restricted to the main detachment zone but pervasively affects the interior of the metamorphic footwall and that retrogressive deformation is not restricted to a single time period but is spread over an extended time period.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a new aspect of retrogressive deformation within and at the upper part of a high-temperatur e metamorphic core complex.
the retrogressive deformation of the footwall of the metamorphic complex, which is a key process in the exhumation of high-temperature metamorphism.
retrogression in a high-temperature, metamorphic core complex.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
retrogression in metamorphic core complexes is a complex process that may involve multiple stages of retrogressive deformation and metamorphic conditions during exhumation.

retrogression within metamorphic core complexes is not only restricted to main detachments and low-angle shear zones but also occurs within the interior of the core complexes, and it is not restricted to the topmost levels of core complexes but may pervasively affect migmatite-grade rocks.
the Naxos core complex is a low-grade retrogressed core complex, which is not unique to this particular case.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the Naxos detachment zone is the youngest of a series of detachments that were active during the late Oligocene−early Miocene and that the retrogressive events in the footwall of the Naxos core complex reflect exhumation of the metamorphic rocks during the late Miocene.

low-angle shear zones, detachment zones, and their footwalls may have been affected by pervasive retrogression during exumation of metamorphic core complex footwalls, and that retrogressive deformation may have occurred in a wide temporal range.

the Naxos retrogression is part of a regional, long-lasting retrogression event in metamorphic core complexes that occurred during the middle−late Miocence and that the timing of this retrogression is related to the retreat of the Hellenic subduction zone.
The main takeaway from our work is that
low-grade retrogression can be pervasive and affect significant portions of a metamorphic core complex.
retrogression is a widespread process during exhumation of metamorphic core-complex footwall areas.
retrogression of high-temperature metamorphosed rocks during exhumation is more widespread and pervasive than previously thought.
